title: APT1
summary: APT1 is the designator given in a widely cited 2013 private-sector report to a long-running intrusion set that the report attributed with high confidence to a specific unit of the Chinese People's Liberation Army, an attribution that has since been debated by other analysts and should be treated as a third-party assessment rather than an established fact. The same activity cluster has been published under names including Comment Crew, Comment Panda, Byzantine Candor, and the Shanghai Group, and later research has questioned whether all of it represents one organisational entity or several overlapping clusters sharing tooling and infrastructure. Open reporting describes a breadth-first targeting model rather than narrow sector focus: hundreds of victim organisations across government, defence, aerospace, energy, technology, media, legal, and consulting sectors, concentrated in the United States and other English-speaking countries, with additional victims reported across Asia and Europe. The tradecraft described is comparatively straightforward and repetitive, which is itself the analytic point. Reporting characterises heavy reliance on spearphishing email with malicious attachments or links as the dominant initial access method, followed by remote access through established footholds, use of publicly available and custom remote administration tooling, credential theft from the local host, and long-dwell collection of email and documents. Persistence has been described through service creation and scheduled execution, and exfiltration largely over the same channels used for command and control. Because tooling overlapped with commodity malware and reused infrastructure, defenders face an attribution problem: overlap does not by itself prove a shared operator. For detection planning, the enduring value of studying APT1 is that it illustrates a high-volume, low-sophistication campaign where classic controls such as email attachment filtering, egress restriction, and rapid detection of remote access tooling still carry most of the defensive weight. Many of the specific indicators published in the original report are long obsolete, so the durable lessons are behavioural, not indicator-based.
objectives: Explain why breadth-first targeting changes how defenders prioritise detection engineering compared with a narrowly sector-focused threat.
Analyse spearphishing attachment and link delivery chains and identify the log sources that reveal each stage of the chain.
Detect unauthorised remote administration tooling installed by a user or malware and distinguish it from sanctioned administrative software.
Explain how long-dwell collection of email and documents is detected through volume and access-pattern anomalies rather than signature matching.
Describe how reused infrastructure and commodity tooling create attribution ambiguity and how to state that ambiguity in a threat assessment.
Evaluate why published indicators decay and design a detection portfolio that survives indicator rotation.
Explain the role of egress filtering and protocol restriction in limiting damage from an established foothold.
